source.title: Mechanistic Decomposition of Sentence Representations
source.authors: Matthieu Tehenan; V. Natarajan; Jonathan Michala; Milton Lin; Juri Opitz

record.tranche_reason: Applies dictionary decomposition to sentence-embedding models and reports recovered token-level features, extending the relevant feature-recovery question to sentence encoders rather than testing the original toy-network setup or LLMs.
record.gate_note: The study does not test superposition under feature-over-dimension capacity pressure, a sparsity-dependent transition, or competition for dimensions. Its dictionary is supervised and its results concern sentence-embedding models. The hyperparameter tables report sweeps used to select configurations; those tuning results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses supervised dictionary learning as an interpretability tool on sentence encoders and reports how well its own method works. Atom–label alignment is pushed by a classification loss on POS/DEP labels. The 64-atom dictionary is undercomplete relative to MiniLM's 384-d embeddings (Appendix C range 384–768). So the results cannot show sparse features beyond the dimension count, features spread across neurons, or superposition in any sense. The study never measures neurons, polysemanticity, capacity, or SAE recovery.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors present a proof of concept that supervised dictionary learning recovers interpretable token-level features in sentence encoders, often preserved linearly through mean pooling. They also conclude from probes that syntactic information is largely linearly encoded. They make no claim about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses supervised dictionary learning on token representations from sentence-embedding models, with linguistic-label supervision and mean-pooling analysis; it does not reproduce the original toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies dictionary size and linear versus nonlinear configurations in its hyperparameter sweep; it fixes sparsity at 5 non-zero coefficients in the stated setup.

fits_no_version.finding: In an undercomplete (64-atom) supervised dictionary on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 token embeddings, top atoms align with single dependency relations (confidence up to 92%). The atoms are nearly orthogonal with a few clusters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised, undercomplete dictionaries on sentence-encoder tokens yield label-aligned, near-orthogonal atoms.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes recover POS from sentence-encoder token embeddings nearly as well as MLP probes (0.89 vs 0.94 on MiniLM).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Syntactic information is largely linearly decodable in sentence-encoder token embeddings (a linear-representation finding, not superposition).

record.problems: The authors describe the work as a proof of concept and note that it covers three sentence-embedding models and a 140 k-token Brown-corpus sample. The evidence does not establish LLM feature geometry or canonicality of learned features; some geometry results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The hyperparameter tables in Appendix E.4 report many configuration-specific validation and label-prediction metrics. They are sweep results used to assess/select configurations, so they were not entered as claim-result rows; the paper does not identify in the text a single table row as the reported best configuration's metric values.

untested.parts: No toy model, no feature-count vs dimension regime, no sparsity transition or geometry of superposed features.
No neuron-level analysis and no capacity competition.
No neuron-level spreading measured. The dictionary is supervised and undercomplete, so it does not test unsupervised recovery of more sparse features than dimensions in LLMs or encoders.
No completeness, stability across seeds, or canonicality tests of atoms. The hyperparameter sweeps vary k but report only reconstruction and F1.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label is dropped. The dictionary is supervised toward the labels it is then judged on, and it has fewer atoms (64) than embedding dimensions (384 for MiniLM). The results therefore carry no evidence about superposed sparse features. The probe results (Figures 2–3) and the hyperparameter tables are not needed as claim rows.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network experiment with more sparse features than dimensions, no sparsity-dependent transition, and no test of the claimed superposition regime.
No test of neurons competing for capacity or of important features receiving dedicated dimensions while others share.
No test of polysemantic neurons or of alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Tests supervised dictionary decomposition of sentence-embedding token representations, not LLM activations or SAE recovery; it does not test whether features are spread across neurons.
No test of whether dictionary atoms are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model.
The learned dictionary represents atoms as vectors, but the study does not test whether the model's underlying features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: all-MiniLM-L6-v2
rows.size_stated: compact BERT-based model; dimensions not stated
rows.operation_detail: Applied supervised dictionary learning to token representations and assessed atom-label specialization.
rows.measure: Interpretability and label-assignment confidence of dictionary atoms
rows.value: The ten atoms with the highest label-assignment confidence each specialize in a single dependency relation; confidence up to 92%.
rows.note: The paper also describes atoms specializing in syntactic features, including adjectival modifiers and numerals.
rows.check: Atom specialization comes from a supervised dictionary trained with a label-prediction loss, and the dictionary is undercomplete (64 atoms vs 384-d). Specialization up to 92% confidence is partly built in by the supervision. It does not show the model contains sparse superposed features that a dictionary or SAE recovers, so it should not be linked to V4.

rows.subject: all-MiniLM-L6-v2
rows.size_stated: compact BERT-based model; dimensions not stated
rows.operation_detail: Measured pairwise cosine similarity among learned dictionary atoms.
rows.value: Off-diagonal cosine similarities are described as near 0; the basis is described as almost orthogonal, with a few tight clusters.
rows.note: The paper names atoms 35–47–16 as an example cluster. This measures the learned dictionary's geometry, not the underlying model's superposition geometry.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. This is the geometry of the learned dictionary, not of the model's features. Near-orthogonality of 64 atoms in 384-d is unremarkable.

rows.subject: all-MiniLM-L6-v2
rows.size_stated: compact BERT-based model; dimensions not stated
rows.operation_detail: Measured atom contributions to pooled sentence representations.
rows.value: The contribution distribution is nonuniform; atoms 0, 9, and 62 are described as dominating. Negative contributions are described as cancellation between atoms, attributed to the dictionary not being fully orthogonal.
rows.note: No numerical contribution values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. Atom contributions to mean-pooled vectors are a result of the study's own method, not a superposition measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence-embedding model, Brown corpus sample, 64-atom linear dictionary
reader_labels.reason: The learned dictionary yields atoms reported to specialize in syntactic features, with label-assignment confidence up to 92% (R1); this is evidence in a sentence encoder, not an LLM or an SAE.
